Chapter 9 · Birth of the discipline · 1834–1880

Psychophysics and measurement

How Weber, Fechner, Helmholtz and Donders turned sensation and reaction time into something that could be measured.

In the mid-nineteenth century many philosophers took it for granted that the mind could not be measured. Kant had argued as much: inner experience has no extension and cannot be submitted to mathematics. Psychophysics was born precisely to challenge that idea with data.

What were people trying to understand?

The question looked simple: what is the relationship between the physical intensity of a stimulus (a weight, a light, a sound) and how intensely we feel it? If that relationship followed a rule, sensation stopped being ineffable and became something that could be studied.

With what methods?

The physiologist Ernst Heinrich Weber asked volunteers to compare weights held in the hand. In his work on touch (1834) he noticed that the smallest difference we notice is not a fixed amount but a proportion of the starting weight: if 100 grams needs a few extra grams before the change is felt, 200 grams needs roughly twice as much. That minimum difference is called the just noticeable difference.

Gustav Theodor Fechner, a physicist and philosopher in Leipzig, took the idea much further. In Elements of Psychophysics (1860) he proposed that sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity, and he systematised three procedures still taught today: the method of limits, the method of constant stimuli and the method of adjustment. For the first time, subjective experience was studied with series of trials, records and calculations.

Who took part?

Besides Weber and Fechner, Hermann von Helmholtz measured the conduction speed of the nerve impulse in 1850, and it turned out to be much slower than expected. If a nerve took measurable time, so would the processes that depend on it. The Dutch ophthalmologist Franciscus Donders used that idea in 1868 in his subtraction method: by comparing the time of a simple reaction with the time of a reaction that required a choice, he estimated how long the choice itself took. Mental chronometry had begun.

What did it contribute?

  • The idea that experience can be studied with repeatable procedures.
  • The concepts of threshold and sensitivity, still basic in audiology, ophthalmology and ergonomics.
  • Reaction time as a window onto processes that cannot be seen.
  • A working model, with instruments, protocols and statistics, inherited by the first laboratories.

What was revised later?

Weber's law works well in the middle ranges but fails at the extremes. Fechner's logarithmic law was disputed from the start, and in the twentieth century Stanley Smith Stevens proposed a power law based on asking people to estimate magnitudes directly. Later, signal detection theory showed that the "threshold" also depends on the observer's criterion: two people with the same sensitivity may say "yes, I notice it" more or less readily depending on what is at stake. Today sensitivity and response bias are kept apart.

Psychophysics did not measure "the soul", but it showed that questions about experience could be asked and answered with experiments.

References

  1. Fechner, G. T. (1860). Elemente der Psychophysik. Leipzig: Breitkopf und Härtel.
  2. Donders, F. C. (1969 [1868]). On the speed of mental processes. Acta Psychologica, 30, 412–431.
  3. Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153–181.
  4. Green, D. M. y Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Nueva York: Wiley.
